description: I am a B.Tech Computer Science student interested in space technology and planetary science. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, I am developing an interactive Mars Geological Exploration platform. It brings together NASA datasets, supporting scientific information, geological exploration, and analytical tools through a unified dashboard, with the goal of making Martian geological data easier to explore, visualise, and understand.
summary:
What it is and why we built it. AREION is an integrated workspace for exploring the Martian surface. Mars data is abundant, but it is scattered across archives with different formats, map projections, resolutions and coverage. Finding what is known about one place means searching many portals and aligning results by hand. We built AREION to solve that integration problem, using Jezero Crater as our case study.

Why it matters. Orbiters reveal regional patterns while rovers examine targets up close, and no single instrument answers every question. Seeing complementary measurements together improves interpretation. AREION keeps source, coordinates, units, coverage and uncertainty attached to every layer and observation, so missing data stays visible and conclusions stay honest.

How it answers the challenge. Built on open NASA data (the NASA Images API, with PDS MOLA, CRISM, THEMIS, Mars Trek and Mars 2020 as research targets), AREION turns scattered archives into one location-led workflow: select a region, discover data, compare evidence, record observations, explore a route. Our working prototype already searches NASA imagery and links user geology notes to NASA Image IDs. Next come a planetary map, terrain layers and route analysis with Dijkstra and A*.
details:
How it works

AREION is a location-led workflow: select a region, discover data, compare evidence, record observations, and explore a route. The working prototype searches NASA’s image library and shows the selected image with its title, date and NASA ID. Users record geological observations (visible material, texture, colour, notes), and each one is stored against its NASA Image ID so every finding can be traced to its source. A planetary map, terrain layers and route analysis are planned next.

Goals

  • Let people explore location-linked Mars datasets together instead of searching separate archives.
  • Keep source, coordinates, units, coverage and uncertainty visible on every layer and observation.
  • Grow in tested stages: foundation, planetary map, terrain and data, analysis, route explorer.

NASA data

  • Working now: the NASA Images API (images.nasa.gov).
  • Research targets, not yet connected: MOLA elevation, HiRISE imagery via Mars Trek, THEMIS thermal data, CRISM spectral data, and Perseverance (Mars 2020) instrument data.

Tools

Python, Gradio, pandas and requests, prototyped in Google Colab. Local development uses VS Code (Python 3.13) with pytest for testing. The route explorer will use Dijkstra and A* algorithms.

AI tools

We used GEMINI Argon 4 for coding guidance. All project decisions and the final content were ours (team).

References and external sources

  1. NASA Perseverance instruments: science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-2020-perseverance/science-instruments/
  2. PDS MOLA archive: pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/missions/mgs/megdr.html
  3. NASA Mars Trek: trek.nasa.gov/tiles/apidoc/trekAPI.html?body=mars
  4. PDS CRISM archive: pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/missions/mro/crism.htm
  5. NASA Odyssey / THEMIS: science.nasa.gov/mission/odyssey/science-instruments/
  6. Mars 2020 PDS bundle: pds.nasa.gov (Mars 2020 mission bundle)
  7. NASA Images API: images.nasa.gov

The Mars globe, rover and route images in the deck are original or schematic illustrations, not NASA photographs or measured data.
